notes.meaning: Solomon became firmly settled on the throne of Israel, and God blessed him with great honor and influence. His strength did not come from his own power, but because the Lord his God was with him every step of the way. When God supports a leader, the whole kingdom rests on a solid foundation.

Solomon called together all the national leaders, army officers, judges, and family heads from across the land. He wanted the entire nation to join him in a public act of worship at the very start of his reign. Good leaders use their influence to guide others toward God.

The king and the leaders traveled to Gibeon because the sacred tent of worship made by Moses was located there. Even though it was set up on a high hill, this tent was the legal center for Israel's worship where God met with His people. Solomon showed deep respect for the sacred history of his nation by going to this holy spot.

The sacred chest known as the ark of God was not at Gibeon, because King David had already brought it to Jerusalem and set up a special tent for it. This meant Israel had two main places of worship at this time. Solomon still honored the ancient tabernacle at Gibeon while planning for the permanent temple in Jerusalem.

The original bronze altar made back in the desert by Bezalel still stood in front of the tabernacle at Gibeon. Because this was the altar God had commanded for sacrifices, Solomon and the leaders came there to seek the Lord's favor and guidance. They made sure to worship God in the way He had instructed long ago.

Solomon presented a thousand burnt offerings on the bronze altar through the priests. Offering such a huge number of animals showed his deep devotion and gratitude for God's generous blessings. He gave back to God freely from the great wealth he had inherited.

During the night after the sacrifices, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and invited him to ask for whatever he wanted. This was both an open promise of blessing and a test to see what Solomon truly valued in his heart. God delights when His people bring their deepest needs to Him in prayer.

Solomon began his answer by praising God for His loyal love and mercy toward his father David. He recognized that sitting on the throne was a gift from God, not something he had earned on his own. Remembering God's past goodness helps prepare our hearts before we make our requests.

Solomon asked the Lord to keep the covenant promise He had made to David about his royal line. The people of Israel had grown so large that they were like the dust of the earth in number. Solomon knew that fulfilling such a heavy calling required God's direct help.

Rather than asking for personal power, Solomon asked for wisdom and understanding to lead and serve the nation well. He openly admitted that he was not able to guide such a massive people without divine guidance. True leadership starts with humble dependence on God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic Bibles include the Book of Wisdom, where chapter 9 contains a longer prayer of Solomon asking for wisdom, showing that divine wisdom is a pure gift of God that must be sought through humble prayer.

notes.meaning: God praised Solomon because his heart's desire was to serve the people rather than gain selfish benefits. He had not asked for riches, fame, long life, or the defeat of his enemies. God sees our true motives and is pleased when our prayers focus on doing His will.

God granted Solomon the wisdom he requested and also promised him extraordinary wealth, possessions, and honor beyond any king before or after him. When Solomon put spiritual gifts first, God generously gave him earthly blessings as well. Seeking God's kingdom first brings His full and gracious supply.

After worshipping before the tabernacle at Gibeon, Solomon returned to Jerusalem to carry out his royal duties. He did not let his new spiritual gifts go to waste, but immediately got to work governing Israel. Worship was his first priority, and faithful service was his next.

Solomon built up a massive military force, gathering fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses into special fortress cities and Jerusalem. While this showed his great power and wealth, commentators note that God's law had warned kings not to stockpile horses. It is easy to rely on military might instead of resting solely in God's protection.

During Solomon's reign, precious metals were so plentiful in Jerusalem that silver and gold seemed as ordinary as rocks on the ground. Valuable cedar wood became as common as everyday sycamore trees. God proved His word true by pouring out astonishing prosperity across the whole nation.

Solomon's royal traders imported fine horses from Egypt and Kue, which was a region in Cilicia. The king set up regular trade routes and established prices to supply his growing army. This trade brought great business profit, but it also opened regular contact with foreign nations that God had cautioned Israel about.

A chariot from Egypt cost six hundred pieces of silver, and a horse cost one hundred and fifty pieces. Solomon's traders also resold these chariots and horses to the kings of the Hittites and the Arameans, making Israel the center of international trade. His wisdom brought immense commercial success to the kingdom.
